t:
(a) 
The Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949 (50 U.S.C. 403a–403j) is amended by adding at the end thereof the following new section:


“authority to pay death gratuities
“Sec. 11. 

(a)

(1) 
The Director may pay a gratuity to the surviving dependents of any officer or employee of the Agency who dies as a result of injuries (other than from disease) sustained outside the United States and whose death—

“(A) 
resulted from hostile or terrorist activities; or


“(B) 
occurred in connection with an intelligence activity having a substantial element of risk.



“(2) 
The provisions of this subsection shall apply with respect to deaths occurring after June 30, 1974.



“(b) 
Any payment under subsection (a)—

“(1) 
shall be in an amount equal to the amount of the annual salary of the officer or employee concerned at the time of death;



“(2) 
shall be considered a gift and shall be in lieu of payment of any lesser death gratuity authorized by any other Federal law; and


“(3) 
shall be made under the same conditions as apply to payments authorized by section 14 of the Act of August 1, 1956 (22 U.S.C. 2679a).”.





 
    (b)

        (1) 
Chapter 75 of title 10, United States Code, relating to death benefits, is amended by adding at the end thereof the following new section:


“§1489. 
Death gratuity: members and employees dying outside the United States while assigned to intelligence duties

“(a) 
The Secretary of Defense may pay a gratuity to the surviving dependents of any member of the Armed Forces or of any employee of the Department of Defense—

“(1) 
who—

“(A) 
is assigned to duty with an intelligence component of the Department of Defense and whose identity as such a member or employee is disguised or concealed; or


“(B) 
is within a category of individuals determined by the Secretary of Defense to be engaged in clandestine intelligence activities; and



“(2) 
who after the date of the enactment of this section dies as a result of injuries (excluding disease) sustained outside the United States and whose death—

“(A) 
resulted from hostile or terrorist activities; or


“(B) 
occurred in connection with an intelligence activity having a substantial element of risk.




“(b) 
Any payment under subsection (a)—

“(1) 
shall be in an amount equal to the amount of the annual basic pay or salary of the member or employee concerned at the time of death;


“(2) 
shall be considered a gift and shall be in lieu of payment of any lesser death gratuity authorized by this chapter or any other Federal law; and


“(3) 
shall be made under the same conditions as apply to payments authorized by section 14 of the Act of August 1, 1956 (22 U.S.C. 2679a).”.





 
        (2) 
The table of sections at the beginning of such chapter is amended by adding at the end thereof the following new item:


“Sec. 1489. Death gratuity: members and employees dying outside the United States while assigned to intelligence duties.”.

fable.w: The section authorizes the CIA Director and the Secretary of Defense to pay death gratuities to the surviving dependents of intelligence personnel. The tempting reading is that the dependents are outside parties dealing with the government, but they are only recipients of a benefit payment, which the definition excludes. There is no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government.
fable.s: The Director may pay a gratuity to the surviving dependents of any officer or employee of the Agency

opus.w: The section lets the CIA Director and the Secretary of Defense pay death gratuities to surviving dependents. That is a benefit payment, and the definition excludes benefits from participation. The Secretary decides who is covered alone, without requiring regulations, hearings, comment or consultation with anyone outside the government. Calling this participation because dependents receive payments would confuse receiving a benefit with taking part in a decision.
opus.s: The Secretary of Defense may pay a gratuity to the surviving dependents of any member of the Armed Forces or of any employee of the Department of Defense
opus.b:
I'm calling this **No** because no one outside the federal government takes part in any decision.

1. **Tempting misreading:** You could read the payments to surviving dependents as outsiders being involved. You could also read the Secretary of Defense deciding which people count as "engaged in clandestine intelligence activities" as a process that needs input. Neither holds up. Paying a benefit is not participation. The Secretary makes that determination alone, with no hearing, comment period, advisory body, rulemaking requirement or consultation. The reference to 22 U.S.C. 2679a only borrows that law's payment conditions.

qwen_chat.w: This section authorizes the payment of death gratuities to surviving dependents of federal employees. The definition of participation explicitly excludes 'applications for benefits or grants.' Paying a statutory benefit to eligible individuals does not involve consultation, coordination, or decision-making input from outside parties. The dependents are recipients of a benefit, not participants in a federal decision-making process.
qwen_chat.s: The Director may pay a gratuity to the surviving dependents of any officer or employee of the Agency who dies as a result of injuries (other than from disease) sustained outside the United States
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that paying "surviving dependents" involves people outside the government, so it constitutes participation. However, the definition explicitly states that participation "does not include applications for benefits or grants." A death gratuity is a benefit paid to eligible individuals, not a process where outsiders consult with or coordinate with the government to influence a decision. The decision to pay is administrative and based on statutory criteria, not on input from the dependents or other outside parties.
